B01.q: Your aunt asks you to make a 2-minute phone video about her home bakery. You arrive at her house. What do you do first?
options: Ask what the video is for, then list the shots you need
Film the bakery's best-looking cakes first, while the light is good
Good footage with no purpose often misses the shots the video actually needs.
Ask her to walk you round and film the whole tour as it happens
A walk-through gives many clips but no plan, so key shots can still be missing.
Pick the music and editing style so you know the mood first
Mood choices come later, once you know the purpose and the shots.
B01.why: Knowing the purpose and your shot list first saves time while filming and makes editing much easier.

B01.q: In Philipp Humm's video, what makes a story moment feel alive?
options: Slowing down on one moment and showing its small details
Moving quickly between many events so the viewer sees everything
Covering everything rushes each moment and leaves no time for the viewer to feel it.
Adding a strong voiceover that explains how the moment felt
Telling the feeling replaces showing it; small visible details carry it better.
Using fast cuts and music to build excitement around the event
Speed adds energy but skips the small details that make a moment feel real.
B01.why: Zooming into a single moment, with its place, action, thoughts, feelings and words, pulls the viewer into it.
B01.video: Give me 9min, and I’ll improve your storytelling skills by 176%

B01.q: In StudioBinder's production process video, what is principal photography?
options: The stage when the crew records the main footage of the film
The stage when the team plans the shots and schedule before filming
That is pre-production, which happens before principal photography.
The stage when extra close-ups are filmed after the main shoot
Those are pickup shots, which come after principal photography.
The stage when the editor puts the footage together in order
Editing is post-production and happens after filming.
B01.why: Principal photography is the main filming period, when the planned scenes are actually recorded.
B01.video: Film Production Explained — The Production Process

B01.q: You film a chai stall owner making tea, but you only have one long clip from across the road. It looks dull. Next time, what should you film?
options: One view of the whole stall, then closer clips of his hands and the glass
A steady wide clip of the whole stall, held while he makes the tea
One wide view shows the place but none of the detail that makes it interesting.
Close clips of his hands, the glass and his face, all from one side
Close clips give detail, but with no view of the stall the viewer never learns where this is.
A medium clip of him at the stall, then another from the same spot
Two similar clips from the same place add no new information.
B01.why: Several clips of different sizes can be cut together to show the whole action clearly and keep it interesting.

B01.q: According to StudioBinder's guide to shot sizes, what does a close shot mainly give the viewer?
options: Detail and emotion, like a face, an expression or busy hands
The setting around the subject and how things are arranged in it
That is what a wide shot gives; a close shot shows detail.
The distance between people and how they move through the space
Wide shots show space and movement; close shots show detail and feeling.
A full view of a person from head to toe, with their clothes
That is a long shot; a close shot is mainly about detail and emotion.
B01.why: Close shots cut out the surroundings so the viewer focuses on small details and feelings.
B01.video: Ultimate Guide to Camera Shots: Every Shot Size Explained

B01.q: In Simon Cade's video on visual storytelling, how is the story mostly told?
options: Through what the characters do and what the camera shows
Through the dialogue, where characters tell each other what happened
Visual storytelling shows the story in pictures and actions instead of telling it in words.
Through a narrator who explains what the viewer cannot see
A narrator tells; visual storytelling lets the camera and actions show it.
Through title cards that set up each new scene before it starts
Cards describe the story; visual storytelling shows it through action.
B01.why: Good visual storytelling lets actions and images carry the meaning, so the viewer understands without being told.

B01.q: A small sari shop wants an Instagram reel. Their buyers are young women scrolling fast on their phones. How should the reel start?
options: Show the most striking sari up close in the first two seconds
Start with the shop's name and logo for the first two seconds
A logo gives a scrolling thumb nothing to stop for; show the product.
Open with a smiling wide shot of the owner welcoming customers
Friendly, but scrollers need to see the product straight away.
Start with a slow pan across the racks to show the whole shop
A slow pan gives no single thing to look at in the first seconds.
B01.why: These buyers want to see beautiful saris quickly, so the strongest image must come first to hold their attention.

B01.q: In DSLRguide's video, what is the main point about camera choices like framing and light?
options: They guide what the audience notices and understands
They decide mainly how expensive and professional the film looks
These choices guide attention and meaning, not just polish.
They are mostly technical settings that the audience never notices
Audiences feel the effect of framing and light even when they don't notice the choice.
They matter only in big productions with a trained crew
Every video, even a phone video, uses these choices to guide the viewer.
B01.why: Every framing and lighting choice tells the audience where to look and how to read the scene.

B01.q: You edit a video of a busy street market with only a music track on it. Something feels missing. What is the best fix?
options: Mix vendors calling and crowd noise in softly under the music
Replace the music with one loud recording of the market crowd
Crowd noise alone can overwhelm; mixed softly under music it keeps both mood and place.
Add a sound effect of a shop bell at each cut to add life
Invented sounds don't match the place; real market sound does.
Keep the music and add a voiceover describing the market
A voiceover tells; the sound of the place lets viewers feel it.
B01.why: Sounds recorded in the place make the viewer believe they are standing in that market.

B01.q: In StudioBinder's short film The Pen, how does the simple story keep moving forward?
options: Each shot adds a new piece of information that leads to the next
Each shot repeats the main idea so the viewer cannot miss it
Repeating doesn't move a story forward; new information does.
Music rises at each scene so the viewer feels the story moving
Music supports a story but the shots themselves carry it forward.
The same place is shown from several angles to keep it familiar
More angles of the same thing add no new information.
B01.why: When every image gives the viewer something new, the story moves forward clearly, even with very few words.

B02.q: Your cousin asks you to make a short video for her small tailoring shop in Pune. What should you decide before you start filming?
options: What customers should remember most, like her quick alterations.
The best camera angle for showing off her sewing machine.
Angles come after you know the main message.
How long the video should be, so it fits Instagram.
Length matters, but the main message comes first.
Which service she is proudest of, and film only that.
Her pride isn't the point; what makes customers choose her is.
B02.why: A single clear takeaway guides every shot you choose. Viewers can remember and repeat it.

B02.q: In the creative brief video, what does the brief make clear early on?
options: Who the video is for and what it has to get across.
How much the video will cost and who will pay for it.
Cost may be listed, but the early point is the audience and the message.
Which scenes will be filmed on which days of the shoot.
That is a shooting schedule, planned after the brief.
What the final video will look like, shot by shot.
That is a storyboard or shot list, made after the brief.
B02.why: The brief names the audience and the objective first, so everyone on the team works toward the same goal.
B02.video: What Is a Creative Brief? How to Write One That Aligns Your Team

B02.q: You are making a video for a sweet shop's Instagram. Most followers scroll quickly on their phones. How do you plan it?
options: Upright frame, sweets shown in the first two seconds, text on screen.
Upright frame, a slow opening on the shop, text added at the end.
A slow opening loses scrollers, and text should appear with the pictures.
Wide sideways frame, sweets shown in the first two seconds, text on screen.
Followers hold phones upright, so a wide frame shows small with black bars.
Upright frame, sweets in the first two seconds, a voiceover instead of text.
Many people scroll with the sound off, so on-screen text is needed.
B02.why: Phone viewers hold the phone upright and decide in seconds. Show the best part fast and add text for people watching on mute.

B02.q: Your uncle wants a video of the family puja to send on WhatsApp to grandparents in the village. They have old phones and slow internet. What do you send?
options: A short edit of a few minutes, saved as a smaller file.
The full recording, saved as a smaller file so it sends faster.
A smaller file helps, but grandparents won't sit through two hours.
A short edit of a few minutes, in the highest quality file.
Large files are slow to send and play on old phones with slow internet.
Ten separate clips of each ritual, each in the highest quality.
Many large files overload slow internet; one short edit is easier.
B02.why: Think about the device and connection your viewers really have. A short, light file actually reaches them.

B02.q: Your video of a potter at a village fair opens on his hands already shaping clay. Friends say they feel lost. What helps most?
options: Add a shot of his stall and him setting up before the clay.
Add a title card saying where and when the fair was held.
Text names the place but viewers still don't see it; show it.
Slow down the shaping shots so viewers can follow what he does.
Slow motion doesn't tell viewers where they are or who he is.
Add a wider shot of the fair crowd after the shaping scenes.
Context must come first to orient viewers, not after they are already lost.
B02.why: Viewers need to know the place and the person first. Then the action makes sense to them.

B02.q: According to the storyboard video, what is a storyboard mainly used for?
options: Planning each shot as a simple picture with a short note.
Writing out the exact words each person will say on camera.
That is a script, not a storyboard.
Listing the equipment needed on each day of the shoot.
That is a kit list.
Showing a rough version of the film to the client at the end.
That is a rough cut; a storyboard is made before filming.
B02.why: A storyboard pairs a rough drawing with a description for each shot, so you can see the video before you film it.
B02.video: What is a Storyboard and How to Make One

B02.q: In the three act structure video, what usually moves a story from its first act into its second?
options: An event that changes things and starts the main action.
A moment where the hero solves the story's biggest problem.
That is the climax, which comes near the end.
A quiet scene that shows the hero's daily life.
That is act one setup, before the turning point.
A summary scene that repeats what has happened so far.
A recap doesn't change anything; a turning point does.
B02.why: Act one ends when something happens that sets the main story going. That turning point pulls viewers into the development.

B02.q: At a friend's bakery opening, guests will leave in ten minutes. You have many cake close-ups but no shot of the ribbon cutting. What do you film now?
options: A wide shot of the owner cutting the ribbon with guests.
A close-up of the scissors and ribbon, held for a few seconds.
A close-up shows detail but not the owner or the guests, so the event isn't clear.
A shot of guests clapping, filmed as they walk out the door.
Their reaction without the cutting leaves out the main moment.
A selfie-style clip of you saying what is happening.
Talking about the moment is not the same as having the moment on film.
B02.why: Get the shots the story cannot work without first. Detail shots can wait or be picked up later.

B02.q: You are editing an interview with a jeweller and want to remove a cough in the middle of her answer. The cut makes her face jump. What do you do?
options: Cover the cut with a shot of her hands setting a stone.
Zoom in slightly on her face after the cut to hide the jump.
A change of size at the cut can look like a mistake; a cutaway hides it better.
Add a quick white flash at the cut.
A flash draws attention to the cut instead of hiding it.
Speed up the clip after the cut so the jump is hard to see.
Speeding up changes how she speaks, and the face still jumps.
B02.why: A related detail shot hides the cut while her voice keeps going. This is why you film details on every shoot.

B02.q: In the shot list video, what does a shot list do with your story outline?
options: Breaks it into specific shots you can film, with size and angle.
Adds the music and sound effects for each part of the story.
That is sound design, not a shot list.
Turns each scene into a short summary for the client.
A summary isn't something you can film.
Lists the locations and times for each day of the shoot.
That is a schedule; a shot list lists shots.
B02.why: A shot list names each shot clearly, so on the day you know exactly what to film and nothing important is missed.
B02.video: What is a Shot List? (and How to Make One)

B02.q: You are filming your grandmother at her 80th birthday for a family video. Which question will give you the best moment on camera?
options: What was this house like when you first came here?
Do you remember a time when this house felt different?
A yes or no question gets a short answer; ask about a specific memory.
How do you feel about turning eighty today?
A big feelings question gets a general answer; a specific memory makes a story.
Can you tell us a little about your life and your family?
Too broad; people don't know where to start.
B02.why: A question that asks her to describe or remember invites a real story in her own words.

B02.q: What does the scripting method in the Think Media video help you do for a short explainer?
options: Grab attention early, cover points in order, end with a next step.
Introduce yourself fully, explain the topic, then thank viewers.
A long introduction loses viewers; hook them first.
Put the most important point last so viewers watch to the end.
Most viewers leave before that; start with the strongest point.
Write the full script and read it word for word without pausing.
Reading it flatly loses people; the method is about structure.
B02.why: A simple structure keeps viewers watching at the start, guides them through the points, and tells them what to do at the end.
B02.video: How to Write a Script for a YouTube Video (Made Easy!)

B02.q: In the AI storyboard video, what do you still do yourself after the AI makes the frames?
options: Check each frame can really be filmed and pick the shots you need.
Add the camera and lens settings to each frame before shooting.
You choose those on the day; the frames are only a planning guide.
Give the frames to the actors so they copy every pose.
Frames guide the shot; they aren't poses to copy exactly.
Rewrite the story so it matches the AI's frames more closely.
The story leads; the frames follow.
B02.why: AI gives you options fast. You decide what’s realistic.
B02.video: How to Make a Storyboard with AI

B02.q: An AI storyboard of your aunt’s pickle stall shows a crowd of fifty customers. There are usually five. What do you do?
options: Redraw it to match what you’ll really see: a few regulars chatting.
Ask the AI to add more people until the frame looks lively.
That moves the plan further from what you can film.
Plan to fill the frame with friends standing around the stall.
A staged crowd feels fake and misrepresents the stall.
Keep the frame for the client and film something simpler on the day.
Planning one thing and filming another defeats the storyboard.
B02.why: A storyboard is a plan for the real shoot, not a wish list.

B03.q: Your cousin will help film the haldi at a family wedding. You give her a written plan. Which line will help her most?
options: Close-up: turmeric being put on the bride's cheek
Get the happiest faces during the haldi, as many as you can
That is a goal, not a shot she can find and frame.
Wide shot: haldi ceremony in the courtyard
It names size and place but not the action or detail she should catch.
Capture the emotional moments of the haldi for the family
Emotional moments is a goal; a shot list needs specific shots.
B03.why: It tells her how close to frame and exactly what to point the camera at. She could film it without asking you.

B03.q: In the video, what does each single line of a shot list describe?
options: One planned shot, with details like framing and action
One scene, with notes on every shot inside it
A scene holds many shots; each line describes only one.
One day of filming, with times and places
That is a schedule, not a shot list.
One edit decision, such as where a clip starts and ends
Edit decisions come later, in post-production.
B03.why: The video shows that each line is one shot, filled in with fields like size, angle and what happens.

B03.q: You make a rough drawing for a shot of a sweet shop owner behind his counter. What must the drawing show clearly?
options: Where the frame edge cuts him, like at the waist
How his face and expression will look in the final film
A rough drawing can't show that; it needs to show the frame.
Where he will stand and how his hands will move
That can be a note; the drawing must show the frame edge, which sets shot size.
The light direction and how bright the shop will look
Light matters, but a quick drawing is for framing.
B03.why: The drawing's job is to show how much of him is in the frame and where he sits. That is what your helper needs to copy.

B03.q: According to the video, what is the main job of a storyboard (a set of drawn frames)?
options: To help the whole team picture the same plan
To fix the exact camera settings before filming
Settings are set on the day, not in a storyboard.
To replace the script when time is short
A storyboard shows shots; it doesn't replace the script.
To record what was actually filmed for the editor
A storyboard is made before filming, not after.
B03.why: The video stresses that rough frames are enough, because the goal is that everyone shares one plan.
B03.video: What is a Storyboard and How to Make One

B03.q: Next Tuesday at 11 am you will interview a tailor in his shop. You visit this Tuesday at 11 am. What should you check?
options: The traffic sound and where the sun comes in then
Whether the shop has room for your tripod, and nothing else
Space is easy to see on any visit; sound and light change by the hour.
What the tailor will wear and how he looks in the shop's light
He can decide his clothes; sound and light need checking at the real time.
Which angles look best, whatever the noise
Noise can't be fixed later; angles come second.
B03.why: Visiting at the same time shows you the real sound and sun you will get. Then you can plan around them.

B03.q: Apart from sound and daylight, what else does the scout checklist in the video ask you to check?
options: Power points, room for gear, and permission to film
The best tripod height and the lens you will use
Those are your own gear choices, not checks of the place.
The actors' availability and their travel times
That is casting and scheduling, not a check of the place.
The weather forecast and the sunrise time on the day
Daylight is already covered; the checklist asks about the place itself.
B03.why: The checklist covers practical things like power, usable space, weather and permissions, so nothing stops you on the day.
B03.video: 8 Keys to Location Scouting Like a Pro

B03.q: For a college project you want to film a vegetable seller at a market. She looks unsure and says, 'Not today.' What do you do?
options: Thank her and go film a different stall instead
Ask once more, and offer to show her the footage before you use it
She has already said no; asking again puts pressure on her.
Film only her hands and the vegetables so she can't be identified
Hands can still identify her, and she said no to being filmed.
Film the stall from the street and blur her face in the edit
She still said no; blurring afterwards doesn't fix that.
B03.why: She has said no, so you accept it politely and move on. People trust filmmakers who respect their answer.

B03.q: In the video's consent conversation, what makes the person's agreement 'informed'?
options: They know how the video will be used and shared
They have signed a form before you start filming
A form without understanding isn't informed.
They were told your name and your college's name
Knowing who you are isn't enough; they need to know how it will be used.
They are an adult who is not being paid to appear
Age and payment don't make consent informed.
B03.why: The video shows the filmmaker explaining the purpose and use of the footage, so the person can truly decide.

B03.q: Tomorrow morning you film a friend's shop opening on your phone. Tonight the battery is at 40% and storage is almost full. What do you do?
options: Charge it fully and move old videos off the phone
Charge it overnight and carry a power bank, leaving storage as it is
Full storage will stop recording partway through the event.
Delete the largest videos and charge it for an hour in the morning
Deleting before copying risks losing videos, and an hour may not be enough.
Lower the video quality so less storage is used
That is a last resort; clearing space first is better.
B03.why: Doing it the evening before means you arrive with full power and room to record. Nothing stops you mid-shoot.

B03.q: At a family function, your first clips look hazy and soft, even in good light. What is the most likely cause?
options: A smudge of fingerprint oil on the lens
The phone is warm from filming for a long time
Heat can slow a phone but doesn't haze the picture.
The video is set to a lower frame rate than usual
A lower frame rate affects smoothness, not haziness.
The tripod is shaking slightly during recording
Shaking gives wobble, not a hazy look.
B03.why: Phone lenses pick up finger marks easily, which makes video look foggy. A quick wipe with a soft cloth fixes it.

B03.q: After filming your nephew's birthday, your phone is full. You have copied the clips to your laptop. What should you do next?
options: Play a few clips, then copy them to a drive as well
Check the laptop copy has every file, then clear the phone
One copy is still a risk; make a second copy before clearing anything.
Upload to the cloud and delete from the phone at once
You haven't checked the upload finished or that the clips play.
Rename the folders so you can find them, then clear the phone
Naming helps, but doesn't check the files play or add a backup.
B03.why: Checking makes sure the copy works, and a second copy protects you if one device fails. Only then is it safe to delete.

B03.q: The WITNESS video talks about keeping video safe. When does it say you should plan for this?
options: Before you film, as part of your planning
On the day, when you reach the location and check storage
That is too late to plan for it.
At the end of the shoot, when you copy the footage
By then the risk has already been taken; plan before you film.
When something goes wrong, such as a lost or damaged phone
Then it is too late to protect the footage.
B03.why: The video explains that keeping footage safe starts before you record, so you know where files will go and how they will be stored.
B03.video: Planning to Preserve Video for Human Rights

B03.q: In the script breakdown video, what happens after the tool tags the cast, props and locations?
options: Every tag is checked against the script before the shoot.
The tags are sent to the crew as the final shoot list.
Unchecked tags can contain errors that affect the whole shoot.
The tags are used to choose actors and locations automatically.
The team decides, after checking the tags.
The tool rewrites each scene so every tag is included.
The tool tags the script; it doesn't rewrite it.
B03.why: Use the AI list as a first draft, then check it.

B03.q: An AI breakdown of your short film misses that a character drinks chai in scene 3. Whose job is it to catch that?
options: Yours, by reading the script against the breakdown.
The director's, who will notice it during the shoot.
That is too late; it should be caught in planning.
The props helper's, who will spot a missing item on the day.
Missing items found on the day cost time; catch them beforehand.
The AI's, if you ask it to run the breakdown again.
A second run can miss it again; a human check is needed.
B03.why: You own the plan, even when a tool helps write it.

B04.q: You are filming a speech at a family function from the back of the hall. You hold the phone in both hands, but the picture still wobbles a lot. What is the most likely cause?
options: You zoomed in a lot, which makes every small movement look bigger.
You are holding the phone too tightly, so your pulse shakes the picture.
A firm grip is right; the wobble grows with zoom, not with a tight hold.
The frame rate is set too high, so every small shake gets recorded.
Frame rate changes smoothness, not how much the picture shakes.
The hall lights flicker, which makes the picture seem to shake.
Flicker causes bands of brightness, not wobble.
B04.why: Zoom makes small hand movements look much bigger. Walk closer and zoom out to get a calmer shot.

B04.q: At a street market, you want to follow your friend as she walks between the stalls. How do you film while moving?
options: Walk slowly with bent knees, both hands holding the phone near your chest.
Walk slowly on your toes with the phone held out at arm's length.
Straight arms and a bouncing walk make the shake bigger.
Walk backwards in front of her, holding the phone low at your waist.
Walking backwards is risky and the phone swings when held low.
Walk quickly to keep up with her, holding the phone with one hand.
Fast steps and one hand shake the picture more.
B04.why: Soft knees soak up your steps, and keeping the phone close to your body makes it steadier.

B04.q: You left a little extra time at the start and end of each clip of your niece cutting her birthday cake. When you edit, what does that extra time help with?
options: It gives you room to start and end each cut cleanly, or add a fade.
It lets you remove shaky moments from the middle of the clip.
Shake in the middle needs its own fix; spare time only helps at the start and end.
It lets you speed the clip up or down without losing the action.
Speed changes depend on frame rate, not on spare seconds at the ends.
It keeps the audio in sync with the picture on the timeline.
Sound stays in sync by itself; spare time doesn't do that.
B04.why: Spare seconds at each end let you choose the exact cut point and join clips smoothly without losing the action.

B04.q: You just filmed a short interview with a sweet shop owner. Before you leave, you play the clip back. What matters most to check?
options: Listen with the sound on, and check that his face is sharp.
Check that the shop name is visible behind him and the clip is steady.
Background and steadiness help, but sound and a sharp face can't be fixed later.
Check that the light on his face is even and the clip is long enough.
Useful, but a clip with bad sound or a soft face has to be re-shot.
Watch it with the sound off, to judge the picture on its own.
Sound is half of an interview, and a bad recording can't be repaired later.
B04.why: Sound and focus problems can't be fixed later. Catching them now lets you film again while he is still there.

B04.q: At an evening sangeet indoors, the dancers look dark and you want their movement to stay sharp. Your shutter speed is 1/250. What do you change?
options: Open the lens to a lower f-number, and raise ISO a little.
Slow the shutter to 1/60 so more light comes in, and keep ISO low.
A slower shutter lets dancing blur; dancers need a fast shutter.
Raise ISO to the maximum and keep the lens closed at f/8.
A high ISO adds heavy grain, and a closed lens lets in even less light.
Switch to auto mode and let the camera pick the settings.
In dim light auto may choose a slow shutter, which blurs the dancers.
B04.why: Opening the lens lets in more light without blurring motion, and a small ISO boost adds the rest with little grain.

B04.q: In the aperture guide, what happens when you change from f/8 to f/1.8? (The f-number shows how wide the lens opening is.)
options: The lens opens wider, more light comes in, and the background gets softer.
The lens opens wider, more light comes in, and the background gets sharper.
A wider opening makes the background softer, not sharper.
The lens closes down, less light comes in, and the background gets softer.
f/1.8 is a wider opening than f/8; a smaller number is a bigger opening.
The picture gets brighter and the zoom moves closer to the subject.
The f-number changes the opening, not the zoom.
B04.why: A smaller f-number means a bigger opening. It brightens the picture and blurs the background more.
B04.video: Ultimate Guide to Camera Aperture and the Exposure Triangle

B04.q: You film inside a home lit by warm yellow bulbs, and everyone looks orange. Based on the white balance video, what do you do? (White balance tells the camera what colour white is.)
options: Set white balance to the indoor bulb setting, around 3200K.
Set white balance to cloudy, around 6500K, to warm the picture.
Cloudy adds even more warmth; indoor bulbs need the cooler setting.
Set white balance to daylight, around 5600K, for natural colour.
Daylight setting leaves the orange cast from yellow bulbs.
Keep auto white balance and lower the saturation in the edit.
Auto can be fooled by one colour of light, and lowering saturation only half fixes it.
B04.why: Matching white balance to the light source makes whites look white, so skin looks natural.
B04.video: Color Temperature Explained: White Balance Fundamentals

B04.q: You are filming earrings for a friend's small jewellery business on your phone. The phone keeps making the cloth behind them sharp, not the earrings. What do you do?
options: Tap and hold on the earrings until it locks, then keep the same distance.
Tap on the earrings once and then move closer to fill the frame.
A single tap can drift, and moving closer can change focus again.
Switch to the ultra-wide lens so everything stays in focus.
Ultra-wide makes the earrings small and distorted; the focus still needs to be locked.
Add more light on the cloth so the phone sees the earrings clearly.
Light helps, but it doesn't tell the phone what to focus on.
B04.why: Locking focus on the product stops the phone from choosing for you. Staying at the same distance keeps it sharp.

B04.q: You want a family group sharp and the temple behind them sharp too. Based on the depth of field video, what do you aim for?
options: Deep focus, using a bigger f-number like f/8 or f/11.
Shallow focus, using a small f-number like f/1.8.
A small f-number blurs the temple behind the group.
Deep focus, using a small f-number like f/1.8 and standing farther back.
Distance helps, but a wide f/1.8 opening still gives shallow focus.
Medium focus, using f/4, with the group standing close to the camera.
Standing close to the camera makes the depth of field shallower, so the temple blurs.
B04.why: Deep focus keeps near and far things sharp. A smaller lens opening, which means a bigger f-number, gives you that.
B04.video: Depth of Field Explained: Guide to Camera Focus

B04.q: You filmed water splashing from a handpump at 60 frames per second. In your editing app it plays at normal speed and does not look slow. What do you do?
options: Slow the clip down to about half speed in the editing app.
Slow it to about 10 percent speed so the splash lasts longer.
There are not enough frames for that, so it would stutter; about half speed is smooth.
Film it again at 30 frames per second for a smoother look.
A lower frame rate can't give slow motion.
Raise the clip's frame rate to 120 in the export settings.
Export settings can't add frames that were never filmed.
B04.why: Filming at 60 only gives you extra frames. You still have to slow the clip in the edit to see the slow motion.

B04.q: The camera settings video goes through resolution and frame rate early on. Why set these before you start filming?
options: They can't be fixed later, so a wrong choice stays in the footage.
They decide the file size, so a low setting only saves space.
They also set how the picture looks and moves, and a wrong choice stays in the footage.
The editing app fixes any mismatch automatically when you import.
The app can't create detail or frames that were never recorded.
Auto mode always picks the best ones, so a quick check is enough.
Auto doesn't know your project; the settings stay in the footage.
B04.why: Some settings are baked into the clip when you record. Checking them first saves you from footage you can't use.
B04.video: Basic CAMERA SETTINGS for beginners filmmaking

B04.q: In the auto framing video, what is the camera’s automatic framing compared with?
options: A shot framed by hand.
A shot filmed on a tripod.
The comparison is with a person framing the shot, not with a tripod.
A shot cropped later in the editing app.
The comparison is with framing while you film.
A shot filmed on a different camera.
It compares automatic framing with framing by hand, not another camera.
B04.why: Seeing both side by side shows when auto framing helps.
B04.video: AI-based Auto Framing with Sony ZV-E1

B04.q: You film a dancer with auto framing on. It keeps her face centred but crops her feet. What matters most here?
options: Her full movement, so frame wide enough to see her feet.
Keeping her face centred, because that is where viewers look most.
For dance, the feet and body carry the movement.
Letting the camera follow her fastest so she never leaves the frame.
Tracking speed isn't the issue; cropping her feet is.
Using auto framing and fixing the crop later in the edit.
You can't add back feet that were cropped out.
B04.why: Frame for the story, not for the feature.

B05.q: You are filming a bride's mehendi ceremony on your phone. You already have a shot of the whole courtyard and one of the bride sitting with her aunts. What shot should you add next?
options: Move in close on her palm as the design is drawn.
Film her face in a medium close-up while the aunts talk.
It is another view of the bride; the story needs the detail of the palm.
Film the courtyard again from another corner for variety.
Another wide shot repeats what you already have.
Film the aunts clapping from the same spot as the first shot.
Same spot, same size: no new information.
B05.why: The pattern on her hand is the heart of the moment. A tight shot lets viewers actually see it after the place and the people are shown.

B05.q: The StudioBinder guide explains each shot size. If you film a friend making dosa, which set of shots covers the activity well?
options: The kitchen, then the cook at the stove, then the batter spreading.
The cook at the stove, then the cook from the other side, then again.
Repeating the same size gives no variety; mix sizes.
Close-ups of the batter, then more close-ups of the dosa and the plate.
All close-ups give detail but no sense of the place or the cook.
Two wide shots of the kitchen and one of the street outside.
All wide shots show the setting; none shows the cooking.
B05.why: Mixing sizes tells the viewer the setting, then the person, then the key moment. Together they tell a complete, clear story.
B05.video: Ultimate Guide to Camera Shots: Every Shot Size Explained

B05.q: You are filming the sunset at Marine Drive. The sky is full of orange clouds and the sea is calm and plain. Where do you put the horizon?
options: Low in the frame, so the sky takes up about two thirds.
High in the frame, so the sea takes up about two thirds.
The sea is plain; the clouds are the interest, so give them the space.
Straight across the middle, splitting sky and sea equally.
A centred horizon splits the picture and makes the sky and the sea fight.
Right at the bottom edge, with almost no sea showing.
Some sea gives the sky a base and shows where you are.
B05.why: Placing the horizon about a third up from the bottom gives more room to the interesting sky. It also looks more balanced than cutting the frame in half.

B05.q: The StudioBinder composition guide talks about lines in a scene, like roads, railings or rows of lamps. How do they help a shot?
options: They lead the viewer's eye towards the subject.
They divide the frame into parts so each part can hold a subject.
Lines can guide the eye; dividing the frame isn't their job.
They show how fast the subject is moving through the scene.
Lines direct attention; they don't show speed.
They make the frame look busy so the viewer looks longer.
Leading lines make a frame clearer, not busier.
B05.why: The eye naturally follows lines in a picture. If they point to your subject, the viewer looks right where you want.
B05.video: Ultimate Guide to Film Composition & Framing

B05.q: At a wedding, you film an uncle giving his blessings. He talks to the interviewer, who stands to the left of your camera, so he looks towards the left of the frame. Where do you place him?
options: On the right side, with open area on the left of the frame.
In the centre, with equal space on both sides.
He looks to one side, so the extra space should be in front of his gaze.
On the left side, close to the edge he is facing.
He would look out of the frame with no room ahead of him.
On the left side, with open space behind him on the right.
Space belongs in front of where he looks, not behind.
B05.why: Room in the direction a person looks feels natural and comfortable. It gives their gaze somewhere to go.

B05.q: You are filming your grandmother telling a story in a medium shot, from the waist up. On your phone screen, there is a big area of empty wall above her head. What do you do?
options: Tilt down or move closer so her head sits just under the top edge.
Zoom in until her head touches the top of the frame.
Touching the top feels cramped; leave a small gap.
Leave it, because the wall shows where she is.
A little headroom is good; a big gap makes her look small and wastes the frame.
Tilt up to include more of the ceiling and the room.
More space above her makes the gap worse.
B05.why: A thin gap above the head keeps the face as the main thing. It avoids both wasted wall and an awkward chop.

B05.q: The StudioBinder guide explains using empty space in a frame. What can a lot of empty space around a small figure make viewers feel?
options: That the person is alone or small in their world.
That the person is angry and about to leave.
Empty space suggests being alone or small, not a particular emotion like anger.
That the scene is happening in a very crowded place.
Empty space suggests being alone, not crowds.
That the person is relaxed and has plenty of time.
Empty space around a small figure suggests being small or alone.
B05.why: Empty space carries feeling. A small person in a large empty frame often feels isolated or lost.
B05.video: Ultimate Guide to Film Composition & Framing

B05.q: You are filming a vegetable seller at a street market. On screen, an electric pole stands right behind his head, as if it grows out of it. What do you do?
options: Step a little to one side so the pole is no longer behind him.
Zoom in so the pole is cropped out of the frame.
Zooming keeps the pole behind his head; move your position instead.
Open the lens wider so the pole blurs, then keep filming.
A blurred pole still looks like it grows from his head; change your angle.
Plan to blur or remove the pole later in the edit.
That is slow and often looks fake; moving a step is quicker.
B05.why: A small change in your position changes what lines up behind the subject. It is the fastest fix for a distracting background.

B05.q: The depth part of the StudioBinder guide shows ways to make a subject stand out. Which of these helps?
options: Put more distance between the subject and what is behind.
Dress the subject in the same colours as the background.
Matching colours make the subject blend into the background.
Close the lens to f/16 so everything is sharp.
A sharp background competes with the subject.
Make the background brighter than the subject's face.
A bright background pulls the eye away from the subject.
B05.why: Space behind the subject adds depth and lets the background soften. The person then stands out clearly.
B05.video: Ultimate Guide to Film Composition & Framing

B05.q: You are editing your cousin's birthday speech. You cut out a long pause, and now his face jumps suddenly. What can hide the jump?
options: Place a shot of the cake candles or listening guests over the cut.
Add a slow cross-dissolve across the cut.
A dissolve blends the two faces and looks ghostly; a cutaway hides the jump.
Speed up the second part of his speech slightly.
That changes how he sounds, and the face still jumps.
Add a fade to black in the middle of the speech.
A fade suggests the speech has ended.
B05.why: A short shot of something else in the room covers the join smoothly. That is why filming extra small shots on the day saves your edit.

B05.q: The StudioBinder video on the 180 degree rule talks about an imaginary line between two people talking. How should you film them so the edit makes sense?
options: Keep the camera on one side of the line for all shots.
Cross the line at a cut, as long as the shots look different.
Crossing the line flips who faces which way and confuses viewers.
Place the camera exactly on the line for a better view of both.
On the line they face the camera and the shots no longer match.
Switch sides whenever the speaker changes.
Switching with each speaker flips directions and confuses the edit.
B05.why: Staying on one side keeps each person on the same side of the screen. Your shots then cut together without confusion.
B05.video: The 180 Degree Rule in Film (and How to Break the Line)

B05.q: The StudioBinder guide on camera movement explains pans and tilts. You want to show a tall temple tower from its base to its top in one shot. Which move fits?
options: A slow tilt, moving the camera upward from the base.
A slow pan, turning the camera from left to right.
A pan sweeps sideways; moving from base to top needs a tilt.
A slow dolly forward, walking towards the temple.
Moving forward makes the tower larger but doesn't scan from base to top.
A quick zoom in and out to cover the whole tower.
A quick zoom is jerky and doesn't follow the tower from bottom to top.
B05.why: A tilt moves the camera up or down from one spot. It is the right choice for showing something tall.

B06.q: You are filming a short interview with a shopkeeper in his small kirana shop. The only strong light comes in through the open front shutter. Where do you seat him?
options: Facing the open shutter, with you standing between him and the street.
Sideways to the shutter, so light falls on one half of his face.
Half of his face would be in deep shadow.
With his back to the open shutter, so the street shows behind him.
His face would be dark against the bright street.
Deep inside the shop, right under the tube light on the ceiling.
Overhead light casts hard shadows under his eyes and nose.
B06.why: The shutter is the strongest light in the shop. When his face points at it, he gets free, even light and the camera sees it.

B06.q: In "The Basics of Lighting for Film", what should you study in a scene before you add any more lights?
options: Which way the light already there is falling, and how soft it is.
How bright the scene is, so you know how many lamps to add.
Direction and softness of the light already there tell you what's missing, not brightness alone.
Which colour filters match the mood you want in the scene.
Mood comes after you understand the light you already have.
Where the brightest spot is, so you can keep it out of frame.
Hiding it doesn't help; understanding its direction and softness does.
B06.why: The video shows that you read the existing light first. Then you only add what the scene really needs.
B06.video: The Basics of Lighting for Film

B06.q: At noon you want to film your grandmother talking in the open courtyard. The sun is overhead and her eyes are in deep black shadows. What do you do?
options: Move her into the shade of the veranda, close to the open courtyard.
Keep her in the sun and shine your phone torch on her face.
A torch is far too weak against noon sun.
Keep her in the sun and ask her to tilt her face up to the sky.
Looking up makes her squint and still leaves harsh shadows.
Move her under a tree where light comes through the leaves.
Dappled light makes bright and dark patches on her face.
B06.why: In the shade, the whole bright sky lights her. That is a big source, so the shadows become gentle and her face looks kinder.

B06.q: In "Cinematic Lighting: Types of Light", a table lamp that you can see inside the frame is called what kind of light?
options: A practical light.
A key light.
The key light is the main light on the subject; a lamp you can see in the shot is practical.
A back light.
A back light sits behind the subject; a lamp visible in the frame is a practical light.
A fill light.
A fill light softens shadows; a lamp visible in the frame is a practical light.
B06.why: A practical is a real lamp that is part of the scene. It adds mood and can also add a little light.

B06.q: In "Cinematic Lighting: Types of Light", what job does the fill light do?
options: It lifts the dark side of the face so shadows are less deep.
It is the brightest light and sets the main look of the face.
That is the key light.
It shines from behind to separate the person from the background.
That is the back light.
It lights the background to add depth behind the person.
That is a background light; fill is for the face.
B06.why: The key light makes shadows. The fill light is weaker and controls how dark those shadows are.

B06.q: You are filming a tailor at his machine next to a window on a cloudy day. Your camera picture looks too dark. What is the best first change?
options: Set a smaller f-number (the size of the lens opening), like f/2.8, and keep ISO low.
Raise the ISO to 3200 and change nothing else.
A very high ISO adds grain; open the lens first.
Use a faster shutter speed so his moving hands look sharper.
A faster shutter makes the picture even darker.
Set a bigger f-number like f/11 to keep the whole machine sharp.
A bigger f-number lets in less light, so the picture gets darker.
B06.why: A smaller f-number means a bigger lens opening, so more light comes in without adding grain. Indoors, this is often the cleanest way to get a bright picture.

B06.q: In "3 Cinematic Looks With Natural Light", how does the filmmaker get three different looks?
options: By changing where the person sits, the exposure, and how daylight bounces.
By adding a small LED light to match the mood each time.
The video relies on natural light only.
By changing the lens and camera for each look.
The look comes from the light, not different gear.
By shooting all three the same way and changing colours in the edit.
The looks are made in front of the camera, not fixed later.
B06.why: The video shows that where you place the person and how you control reflected daylight can change the whole mood, with no extra lights.

B06.q: At a haldi function, the couple stands in front of a bright garden in afternoon sun. On your phone, their faces look almost black. What do you do?
options: Move around them so the sun falls on them from the side.
Zoom in closer so their faces fill more of the frame.
Zooming doesn't change the light; the phone still exposes for the bright garden.
Tap on the bright garden so the phone sets exposure there.
That makes their faces darker still.
Keep shooting and plan to brighten the faces in the edit.
Dark faces lose detail that can't be brought back.
B06.why: When the sun is no longer behind them, it lights their faces. The phone can then set brightness for them, not for the sky.

B06.q: At Marine Drive, you want a dancer to appear as a dark outline against the orange sunset sky. How do you set it up?
options: Keep the sunset behind her and tap the bright sky to set exposure.
Keep the sunset behind her and tap on her face to set exposure.
Exposing for her face turns the sky white and loses the orange.
Turn her around so the setting sun shines right on her face.
Her face would be lit, so there is no dark outline.
Keep the sunset behind her and turn on the phone flash.
The flash lights her face and ruins the outline.
B06.why: Setting brightness for the sky makes the person go dark. Light from behind is a mistake for interviews but a useful tool when you want this look.

B06.q: You film a boutique owner with a big window on her left. The right side of her face is too dark. You have a white thermocol sheet. Where does it go?
options: On her right side, just out of frame, tilted to catch the window light.
Behind her head, just out of frame, facing towards the camera.
It bounces light onto her back, not onto her face.
On her left side, right next to the window.
The window side is already bright; the dark side needs the light.
Held above her head, pointing down, just out of frame.
Light from above creates shadows under the eyes and doesn't reach her dark cheek.
B06.why: The sheet must sit on the shadow side and face the light. Then it sends window light back into the dark side of her face.

B06.q: In "The One Dramatic Lighting Technique You Need to Know", what is negative fill?
options: A black surface near the subject that makes the shadow side darker.
A white card near the subject that makes the shadow side lighter.
That is a bounce or fill card, the opposite of negative fill.
A dark filter on the lens that makes the whole frame darker.
Negative fill works on the shadow side only, not on the whole frame.
A coloured gel over the light that makes the shadows bluer.
Colour doesn't change how deep the shadow is.
B06.why: A black surface soaks up light and stops it bouncing back onto the face. This makes the shadows deeper and the look more dramatic.
B06.video: The One Dramatic Lighting Technique You Need to Know

B07.q: You are filming a vegetable seller at a market, and your phone stays 3 metres away for a wide shot. A friend lends you his costly camera-top mic. You also have cheap wired earphones with a mic. Which gives the clearer voice?
options: The cheap earphone mic, clipped to her collar.
The costly mic on top of your phone, with the gain turned up.
It is 3 metres away; turning up the gain also raises the market noise.
The phone's built-in mic, set to the widest pickup.
A wide pickup at that distance records the whole market, not her voice.
The costly mic, moved to a tripod 2 metres from her.
Still far; the voice gets weaker and the noise stays.
B07.why: A cheap mic near the mouth hears the voice strongly over the noise. A costly mic far away hears the whole market.

B07.q: The WITNESS video is about getting good sound on a phone. What is a good habit before you film someone speaking?
options: Make a short test recording and play it back.
Check the recording light is on and the battery is full.
That shows it is recording, not that the sound is good.
Ask the speaker to say their name once while you watch the meter.
The meter shows level only; you must also listen for noise and clarity.
Wear the earphones while recording and play it back in the edit.
Problems found in the edit are too late to fix.
B07.why: A quick test and playback lets you hear noise or a weak voice while you can still change things.
B07.video: An Activist's Guide to Mobile Video — Sound Recording

B07.q: You test the mic on your uncle before his birthday speech. When he laughs, the meter jumps into the red at 0. What do you do?
options: Lower the input level a little, then test his laugh again.
Lower the level a lot so nothing ever reaches the red, then start.
Too low adds hiss when raised later; lower it a little and test.
Keep the level and ask him not to laugh loudly.
You can't control a natural laugh; set the level for it.
Leave it, since the edit can turn loud sounds down.
Clipped sound is distorted for good and can't be repaired.
B07.why: The loudest moments must stay below 0, so you leave some space for laughs and shouts.

B07.q: You record a shop owner talking softly. The meter barely moves and sits around −40. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the level or bring the mic nearer, then test again.
Raise the level in the edit by 20 decibels.
Making it louder later also raises the hiss.
Turn the level up until normal talking touches 0.
Peaks will go into the red; aim for a healthy level below it.
Ask her to speak louder and move to a quieter corner.
Asking a soft speaker to speak up changes how she sounds; fix the mic instead.
B07.why: Speech should sit in the healthy middle of the meter, roughly −15 to −9, so it is clear but safe.

B07.q: You are recording an interview in a small cafe. Through your headphones you hear a faint buzz that was not there before. What do you do?
options: Pause, find the cause, fix it, then carry on recording.
Keep going and plan to remove the buzz later.
Buzz is hard to remove without harming the voice.
Take off the headphones since the meter still looks fine.
The meter doesn't show buzz; your ears do.
Finish the interview, then record the buzz alone for the editor.
A recording of the buzz doesn't remove it from the interview.
B07.why: Hearing a problem during the shoot means you can still fix it, often by moving a cable or switching off a fan.

B07.q: While listening, you hear a rubbing sound each time the speaker moves her hands. What is the best next step?
options: Stop, adjust the clip mic, and ask her that question again.
Ask her to keep her hands still for the rest of it.
That is unnatural and doesn't fix the part already recorded.
Carry on, then re-record just that answer as a voiceover.
A voiceover won't match the room sound or her face.
Ignore it, since viewers will be watching her face.
Viewers hear the rubbing even when they watch her face.
B07.why: The rubbing usually comes from clothing touching the mic, so fix the mic and redo the spoiled answer.

B07.q: At an outdoor wedding, you set up for a speech near a running generator. You hardly noticed it while setting up. What do you do?
options: Move the speaker away or ask for it to be off briefly.
Record as planned, since software can remove hum.
Software removes steady hum only roughly and harms the voice.
Turn the mic level down so the generator sounds quieter.
It lowers her voice as much as the generator.
Put a foam cover on the mic and keep recording.
A cover reduces wind, not a steady engine noise.
B07.why: Dealing with noise before you press record is far easier than trying to clean it afterwards.

B07.q: In the Deity video on hiding a clip mic, what is the main thing to avoid when putting it under clothing?
options: Fabric rubbing or moving against the top of the mic.
The mic touching the shirt at all, so leave it loose.
A loose mic moves and rubs; it should be held firmly in place.
Any cable showing, even if it means burying the mic deep.
Burying the mic deep muffles it; a bit of visible cable is fine.
Putting the mic too close to the speaker's mouth.
Close is good; it is the rubbing that spoils the sound.
B07.why: Hidden mics pick up rustle from cloth, so the mic must be held steady so fabric cannot rub it.
B07.video: How To Hide A Lav Microphone

B07.q: Based on the RØDE video, what should you do before recording speech outside on a windy day?
options: Put a foam or furry cover on the mic.
Turn the mic level up so the voice beats the wind.
Wind noise rises with the level too.
Turn the mic to face the wind so it picks up the voice better.
Facing the wind makes it worse.
Record normally and cut the wind sound in the edit.
Wind rumble is mixed into the voice and can't be cut out cleanly.
B07.why: A cover, plus shelter from a wall or your body, stops wind hitting the mic before it is recorded.
B07.video: Reduce Wind Noise When Recording Outside

B07.q: You finish an interview in a living room with a ceiling fan running. You want to record the quiet sound of the room. What do you do?
options: Keep the fan on as it was and ask everyone to stay silent.
Switch the fan off first so you get a cleaner silence.
The room tone must match the sound under the interview.
Change the fan to a quieter speed, then record the room.
The room tone must match the fan sound used in the interview.
Ask people to chat softly so it sounds natural.
Chat isn't room tone; it adds voices you can't use.
B07.why: This recording is used under cuts, so it must sound exactly like the background during the interview.

B07.q: In the edit, you cut out a long pause. Now the background sound suddenly drops to dead silence for a moment. How do you fix it?
options: Place the quiet recording from that same room under the gap.
Lay soft music over that part to cover the silence.
Music changes the mood; the gap needs the room's own sound.
Add the sound of a different room, as long as it is quiet.
Different rooms sound different, and viewers feel the mismatch.
Leave it, since a short silence is too quick to notice.
A sudden drop to dead silence is noticeable and feels like a mistake.
B07.why: Filling the gap with matching background sound makes the cut smooth and invisible to the ear.

B07.q: You are filming a sweet shop owner for her shop's video. She keeps stumbling and looks worried. What do you say?
options: "No hurry. Just tell me how you started the shop."
"Don't worry, we can fix any mistakes in the edit."
It reassures her, but gives her nothing easy to talk about.
"Try to stop saying umm, it spoils the video."
Pointing out mistakes makes her more nervous.
"Let's stop and try again after you've practised what to say."
Practising raises the pressure; start with an easy question.
B07.why: A relaxed, easy question lets her talk as she normally would, and you can always take it again.

B07.q: In the WITNESS formal interview setup, where does the interviewer sit?
options: Right next to the camera, at about lens height.
Just beside the camera, but standing taller than the speaker.
Looking down at the speaker makes them look small; match eye height.
Far off to one side, so they stay out of the way.
The speaker would look away from the lens.
Directly in front of the speaker, between them and the camera.
That blocks the camera's view of the speaker.
B07.why: Sitting next to the lens gives the speaker a steady, natural eyeline and lets the interviewer keep watching and listening.
B07.video: Interviewing Techniques — The Formal Interview Setup

B08.q: You filmed your cousin's sangeet on a memory card and copied it to your laptop. You need the card again tomorrow. What do you do before you erase the card?
options: Compare the number of files on both, then play a few clips on the laptop.
Check that the folder sizes match, then erase the card.
Matching size doesn't prove every clip plays.
Play the first and last clip on the laptop, then erase the card.
Two clips can't show whether every file came across.
Copy the files a second time to the same laptop folder, then erase.
A second copy on the same drive isn't a real backup.
B08.why: Matching file counts shows nothing was left behind, and playing clips shows the files are not damaged. Only then is it safe to erase the card.

B08.q: The WITNESS video explains video metadata. What is it?
options: Information saved inside a clip, like the date, time, place and device used.
The effects, transitions and titles you add to a clip while editing.
Edits are not metadata; metadata is saved inside the clip by the camera.
The sound and picture settings you choose when you export.
Export settings are not saved inside the original clip.
The folder names and clip labels you create while organising.
Those are your own labels, not what the camera saved in the file.
B08.why: Metadata is the hidden record of when, where and how a clip was made. It can prove a clip is real, but it can also reveal private details like location.

B08.q: You recorded a shopkeeper's interview with a separate mic. The file is called shopkeeper_voice.wav. Your folders are Video, Sound, Music and Exports. Where does it go?
options: Sound, because it is a recording of a voice.
Video, because the interview was filmed at the same time.
The file is a voice recording, so it belongs in Sound.
Music, because Music and Sound are both audio.
Music holds songs; a voice recording is its own kind of sound.
Exports, because it is something you will send to the client.
It is raw material, not a finished file made from the edit.
B08.why: Voice recordings and room sound belong in Sound, while songs go in Music. Sorting by type means you know exactly where to look.

B08.q: You export a first draft of a reel for a local bakery to show the owner. Your folders are Video, Sound, Music and Exports. Where do you save the draft?
options: In Exports, with the other finished files you make from the edit.
In Video, because the draft is a video file like the clips.
Exports keep finished files apart from raw clips.
On the desktop, so it is quick to find and send on WhatsApp.
Files left on the desktop get lost and mixed up.
Back in the project folder, so the draft stays with the edit.
Exports hold things made from the edit, kept apart from the project files.
B08.why: Exports holds everything that comes out of the editor, and Video holds only what came from the camera. Keeping them apart means you never confuse a draft with a raw clip.

B08.q: You finished editing a friend's birthday video. Your laptop is almost full, and many clips were not used. What do you do?
options: Keep every clip, and move the project to an external drive if space is short.
Delete the unused clips, since the edit is already finished.
You may need them for changes, and you can't get them back.
Delete all the clips and keep only the exported video.
The export can't be edited again; the raw clips are the source.
Keep the clips but delete the project file to save space.
The project file is small and holds your edit; deleting it saves little.
B08.why: The original clips are the raw material you cannot film again. Move them to save space, but never throw them away.

B08.q: You want to brighten a clip in a phone app that saves over the file. You have only this one copy of the clip. What do you do?
options: Make a duplicate of the clip first and make changes on the duplicate.
Edit the clip directly, because you can undo it if needed.
Undo may not survive closing the app, and the file is overwritten.
Edit it, but first send the old one to yourself on WhatsApp.
WhatsApp compresses the video, so it isn't a true copy.
Edit it and use the app's reset button if you don't like it.
An app that saves over the file may not be able to restore the original.
B08.why: Working on a duplicate means the original stays exactly as it was filmed. If the change goes wrong, you still have the real clip.

B08.q: You just imported all the clips from a small shop shoot into your editor. Before you start cutting, what do you do?
options: Play a few clips from each bin to see they open with picture and sound.
Delete the clips from your laptop folder, since they are now in the project.
The project only links to the files; deleting them breaks it.
Start cutting straight away, as any problem will show up later.
A bad clip found halfway through costs more time.
Check each clip's name and metadata in the project panel instead of playing it.
Names don't show whether a file opens or has sound.
B08.why: A quick test now catches missing or broken files early. Editors point to your files on the drive, so they must stay where they are.

B08.q: In "Get to know Premiere", you learn the main panels. Which panel do you use to watch a clip and choose a part of it before it goes into your edit?
options: The Source panel.
The Program panel.
The Program panel plays your edit from the timeline, not a single clip.
The Timeline panel.
The Timeline is where you arrange clips after choosing them.
The Project panel.
The Project panel lists your clips; it isn't where you choose a part of one.
B08.why: The Source panel lets you preview a single clip and mark the part you want. The Program panel then shows how your edit looks.

B08.q: The Adobe video "Create a project and import a clip" shows the basic steps. What must you do before you can bring a clip in?
options: Create a new project, giving it a name and a place to save it.
Drag the clip onto the timeline before any project exists.
A clip needs a project to go into.
Open the clip in the Program panel to load it first.
The Program panel shows your edit; it doesn't load clips.
Choose the export settings for the final video first.
Export settings come at the end, not before importing.
B08.why: The project is the container that holds all your clips and edits. Once it exists and is saved somewhere sensible, you can import into it.
B08.video: Create a project and import a clip

B08.q: On 14 March you sent a client a file called shop_reel_v02_2025-03-14. On 16 March you finish their changes. What do you call the new file?
options: The date is new but the version number is old, so it looks like the same file.
The version is new but the date is old, which is confusing.
shop_reel_final_2025-03-16
'Final' doesn't tell versions apart; later changes would need 'final2'.
B08.why: Both the version number and the date need to move forward. Then anyone can tell which file is newest at a glance.

B08.q: Your edit is working well, but you want to try a big change to the music. How do you save your project before you start?
options: Use Save As and give the project the next version number.
Keep saving over the same file and use Undo if needed.
Undo may not go back far, and saving over loses the old version.
Save a copy called backup in the same folder.
An unnumbered 'backup' gets overwritten or confused with later ones.
Turn on auto-save so changes are never lost.
Auto-save overwrites the old version you may want back.
B08.why: A new numbered version keeps the working edit safe. If the change does not work, you simply open the earlier number.

B09.q: You have just imported 40 clips from your cousin's engagement into a free editor. You want to watch one clip closely before using it. What do you do?
options: Click it in the clip area so it plays in the viewer
Add it to the timeline and press play to watch it.
That puts it in your edit before you have checked it.
Right-click it and choose Export so you can play it.
Export makes a new file; it doesn't preview a clip.
Open it from your phone's gallery instead of the editor.
The viewer lets you check a clip without leaving the editor.
B09.why: You can check any clip in the viewer before you decide to put it on the timeline.

B09.q: In the DaVinci Resolve introduction, what is the basic path a clip takes during a first edit?
options: Imported into the media pool, then placed on the timeline and watched
Placed on the timeline first, then imported into the media pool.
A clip must be imported before it can be placed.
Imported into the media pool, then exported, then placed on the timeline.
Export is the last step, not the middle.
Watched in the viewer, then exported, then imported once again.
Importing comes first, and export last.
B09.why: The video follows clips from import into the media pool, onto the timeline, and into the viewer to check the edit.

B09.q: You filmed a friend's chai stall and have three wide shots of the counter. One is sharp and still, one is shaky and one has a scooter passing in front. What do you do?
options: Use the sharp, still one and leave the other two out
Use the sharp one and the shaky one, to give the stall more energy.
Shake looks like a mistake, not energy.
Use the one with the scooter because it shows the street is busy.
The scooter hides the counter, which is the subject.
Use all three so the stall gets more screen time.
More screen time with weak clips makes the video worse.
B09.why: When shots repeat, keep the best one. Fewer good clips make a stronger video.

B09.q: In the Adobe video on adding clips, why do you mark In and Out points before adding a clip to the sequence?
options: So only the part you chose goes into the sequence
So the clip plays faster once it is on the timeline.
In and Out points choose a part; they don't change playback speed.
So the clip's colour stays the same after export.
Colour doesn't depend on In and Out points.
So the app can find the clip again if it is moved.
In and Out marks choose a part; they don't track file locations.
B09.why: In and Out points mark where the useful part starts and ends, so only that part goes into the rough cut.

B09.q: Your clip of a mehndi design starts with three seconds of you adjusting the phone. Then the artist begins drawing. What do you do?
options: Drag the clip's start in until the drawing begins
Keep it so viewers can see how you set up.
Setting up the phone isn't part of the story.
Delete the whole clip and use a different one.
The clip is fine once the start is trimmed.
Add a fade-in over the three seconds so the setup looks smooth.
A fade makes the wasted seconds feel longer; trim them.
B09.why: Pulling in the start removes the dull setup and keeps the good part of the clip.

B09.q: In Adobe's "Trim a clip" video, how is a clip on the timeline made shorter?
options: By dragging its start or end edge inward
By changing its speed so it plays faster.
Speeding up changes how it looks; trimming shortens it.
By cropping the picture to a smaller frame.
Cropping changes the picture size, not the length.
By splitting it and keeping both halves.
Splitting doesn't shorten the clip; you must remove or trim a part.
B09.why: Trimming means pulling in the head (start) or tail (end) of a clip so less of it plays.

B09.q: You are editing a short video for a small sweet shop. You have a wide shot of the shop, a close-up of jalebis frying and a medium shot of the owner serving. Which shot do you show first?
options: The wide shot of the shop, so viewers know where they are
The jalebi close-up, with the wide shot at the very end.
Viewers should know where they are before the detail.
The medium shot of the owner, so people meet him first.
Viewers still wouldn't know where he is.
Any order works, as long as all three shots are used.
Order changes what the viewer understands.
B09.why: A wide shot sets the scene. Closer shots then show detail that viewers can now place.

B09.q: In StudioBinder's "Six Essential Film Editing Techniques", what should you ask yourself about each cut?
options: Does it move the story on or guide where the viewer looks?
Does it add a new and eye-catching transition effect?
Effects draw attention to the cut instead of the story.
Is it about the same length as the shot just before it?
Equal lengths make an edit feel mechanical.
Does it land exactly on the beat of the music?
Beat matching is a style choice; the question is purpose.
B09.why: The video shows that good cuts have a purpose. They push the story forward or direct attention.

B09.q: You are editing an interview with a tailor. In the middle of one answer, he coughs and pauses for five seconds, then continues. What do you do?
options: Cut out the cough and pause and join the two parts
Keep it all in so the interview feels honest.
A cough and a five-second pause slow the answer without adding meaning.
Turn the music up loud to cover the cough.
Loud music distracts and doesn't remove the pause.
Mute the cough and keep the five-second pause.
The pause still slows the interview.
B09.why: Removing the cough and pause keeps his words clear and the video tight.

B09.q: In a family video, your aunt starts a sentence, laughs, says "wait, let me say that again", then says it well. What do you keep?
options: Only the second, clean version of the sentence
Both versions, so nothing she said is lost.
Repeating the sentence makes the answer longer without adding anything.
Only the first try, because it felt more natural.
The first try was the one she stopped and corrected.
The first half of the first try joined to the end of the second.
Joining halves of two takes usually sounds jumpy.
B09.why: When someone restarts, keep the take they finished cleanly and cut the false start.

B09.q: Your 45-second reel for a flower market feels slow. Each shot opens with a second of nothing happening, and two shots show the same marigold stall. What is the best fix?
options: Trim the empty second off each shot and keep one marigold shot
Speed every clip up to double speed and keep them all.
Double speed makes the footage look rushed and keeps the repeat.
Add a fast song and leave the clips just as they are.
Music doesn't remove the empty seconds or the repeat.
Trim the empty seconds but keep both marigold shots.
Two shots of the same stall repeat the same information.
B09.why: Removing dead time and repeated shots makes the video feel quicker without looking rushed.

B09.q: In Every Frame a Painting's "How Does an Editor Think and Feel?", how does an editor decide when to cut?
options: By feeling when the moment has done its job
By using a fixed number of seconds for every shot.
Fixed lengths ignore what is happening in each shot.
By cutting only when the music hits a beat.
Music can guide a cut, but the moment decides it.
By waiting until the speaker finishes every line completely.
Editors often cut before a line ends.
B09.why: The video explains that editors trust their feeling of the moment and the performance to choose the cut point.
B09.video: How Does an Editor Think and Feel?

B09.q: In the text-based editing video, what do you check after cutting from the transcript?
options: The pacing and the cut points, by watching the edit.
Only the spelling in the transcript.
Spelling doesn't show whether the cuts feel smooth.
Nothing. The text cut is final.
A text cut still needs checking by watching it.
Only that the transcript matches the audio word for word.
Matching words doesn't show whether the cuts feel smooth.
B09.why: The transcript speeds up the rough cut. Watching makes it good.

B09.q: The transcript says your interviewee said “two years”, but they actually said “ten years”. What do you do?
options: Fix the transcript and keep their real words in the edit.
Leave it. Nobody reads the transcript.
The transcript drives your edit; a wrong word can mislead you.
Cut that part out to be safe.
Removing a real statement because of a typing error loses content.
Change the edit to match the transcript.
Never change what someone said to match text; fix the text.
B09.why: Check transcripts against what was really said.

B10.q: You are editing a video for a small tailoring shop. You have the owner's interview, a voice-over you recorded later, the hum of sewing machines and a soft song. Where does your voice-over go?
options: On the voice track, together with the owner's interview.
On a new track of its own, set quieter than the interview.
Dialogue belongs together on one track so you can mix all the voices as a group.
On the music track, since it was added later in the edit.
The track follows what the sound is, not when you added it.
On the machine hum track, since it was not filmed on the day.
The voice-over is dialogue, so it goes with the other voice.
B10.why: Tracks are grouped by the kind of sound, not by when it was recorded. All speech sits together, so you can set every voice level in one place.

B10.q: In the DaVinci Resolve audio introduction, what part of the sound is worked on first?
options: Getting the spoken dialogue clean and clear.
Picking and placing the background music.
Music comes after the voices are clear.
Adding sound effects to build the mood.
Effects come later; the dialogue must be clear first.
Setting the final loudness of the whole mix for export.
Loudness comes at the end; voices come first.
B10.why: Speech carries the story, so it is cleaned up first. Music and effects are then added around it.

B10.q: You interview a bakery owner. Before one answer, she is quiet for about four seconds while she thinks. What do you do in the edit?
options: Shorten the gap so her answer comes soon after the question.
Remove the gap completely so her answer starts at once.
With no pause the answer feels rushed; a short beat is natural.
Leave the full gap because it shows she is a real person.
Four seconds feels like a mistake, not a person thinking.
Lay music over the gap so it does not feel empty.
Music hides the pause but doesn't fix the slow pace.
B10.why: Taking out dead air keeps the pace up. The speaker sounds confident and the viewer stays interested.

B10.q: A speaker coughs in the middle of a sentence and you cut the cough out. What should you do next?
options: Play it back and listen that the words around the cut sound natural.
Cut out every tiny pause in the sentence so it plays faster.
Taking out every pause makes the speech sound rushed and robotic.
Raise the volume of the whole clip to cover up the edit.
Louder doesn't hide a bad cut.
Check that the waveform looks smooth around the cut.
A smooth waveform doesn't prove it sounds natural; you have to listen.
B10.why: A careless cut can chop the start or end of a word. Listening back makes sure the speech still flows.

B10.q: Your clip of a busy Diwali street ends, and the next clip is a quiet living room. The street noise stops dead at the cut. What do you do?
options: Bring the street sound down smoothly over about a second as it ends.
Make the whole street clip quieter from start to finish.
The street should stay lively; only the end needs easing.
End the street sound sharply and start the room sound straight away.
A sudden swap still sounds like a jump.
Move the cut one frame earlier on the street clip.
One frame is too short to change how the jump sounds.
B10.why: A gentle drop in volume at the end hides the sudden stop. The change to the quiet room then feels smooth.

B10.q: In the Adobe transitions video, what problem does the audio transition fix?
options: A sudden jump in the sound where two clips meet.
A voice that is too quiet next to the music.
That is a level problem, fixed by balancing.
A low hiss that runs under the whole clip.
That needs noise reduction, not a transition.
Sound that is out of sync with the picture.
Sync is a different problem from a jump in sound.
B10.why: An audio crossfade blends the end of one clip into the start of the next. This removes the harsh jump at the edit.
B10.video: Elevate your project with cinematic video transitions

B10.q: You made a phone video for a sari shop with the owner talking over a lively instrumental. Friends say they cannot make out what she says. What do you change?
options: Lower the music a lot while she talks, then check on a phone speaker.
Push her voice up until the level meter goes into the red.
The voice will distort.
Lower the music just a little so it still feels lively.
