A little isn't enough to make the voice clear.
Replace the music with a different lively song.
Another busy song has the same problem.
B10.why: The words matter most here, so the music must sit clearly below the voice. Checking on a phone speaker shows how most viewers will hear it.

B10.q: In "Mix audio like a pro", what does the ducking section show?
options: The music drops in volume on its own whenever someone speaks.
The voice is pushed up to the loudest level it can go.
That is raising the voice, not ducking.
Background noise is removed from the voice recording.
That is noise reduction, not ducking.
The music is replaced by room sound while someone speaks.
Ducking lowers the music; it doesn't swap it.
B10.why: Ducking (automatic lowering of one sound when another plays) keeps music from competing with speech. The music returns when the talking stops.

B10.q: In "Perfect your audio mix", your music is longer than your video. What does the video show you can do?
options: Change the music's length so it fits and ends with the video.
Speed up the video so it lasts as long as the music.
That changes the picture instead of fixing the music.
Speed up the music so it ends with the video.
That changes the music's tempo and pitch.
Let the music cut off wherever the video happens to end.
An abrupt stop feels wrong; the music should end with the video.
B10.why: The video shows the music being adjusted to the right length. It then finishes neatly with the picture.

B10.q: You film a chai seller at a railway station pouring tea from high up into a glass. What do you do with the sound?
options: Keep the recorded pour along with the station noise around it.
Mute the clip and play only a cheerful song over it.
The real sound is what makes the place feel alive.
Swap in a clean pouring sound from a free library.
A made-up sound doesn't match the place.
Keep the pour but remove the station noise around it.
The station noise tells viewers where they are.
B10.why: The splash of tea and the station bustle put the viewer right there. Sound that matches the picture makes the scene believable.

B10.q: You add a voice-over to a video of a vegetable market. What do you do with the market sounds?
options: Keep them low under the voice and let them rise in the gaps.
Remove them fully so the voice-over is very clear.
Silence feels empty; keep the place's sound low.
Keep them the same low level the whole time.
A constant low level feels flat; let them rise in the gaps.
Keep them as loud as the voice so it feels busy.
They would fight with the voice.
B10.why: Soft market sound keeps the scene alive without hiding the words. In the pauses it can come up and fill the space.

B10.q: A café owner wants a popular film song in their Instagram ad. They say it is fine because they bought it on a music app. What do you do?
options: Explain buying only allows listening, and suggest licensed music.
Use the song, since the owner has already paid for it.
Buying a song to listen to doesn't give rights to use it in an ad.
Use only thirty seconds, since short clips are allowed.
There is no safe length.
Use a cover version recorded by someone else.
A cover still needs the song's rights.
B10.why: Publishing music needs permission for that use. Licensed library music keeps the ad from being muted or taken down.

B10.q: You find a track on a free music website for a client's video. What should you check before using it?
options: Read its licence to see if it allows your kind of use.
Check that the artist's name is shown on the page.
A name on the page is not permission.
See that the track has been downloaded many times.
Many downloads don't mean it is allowed.
Make sure the site's home page uses the word free.
The word free on a website doesn't say what each track allows.
B10.why: Each track's licence says how you may use it, like whether business use is allowed or credit is needed. Checking it protects you and your client.

B10.q: In the speech enhancement video, how do you decide how much clean-up to use?
options: Compare with the original and keep the voice sounding natural.
Always turn it up to the highest setting for the cleanest sound.
The strongest setting makes voices thin and robotic.
Use whatever setting the tool picks for you automatically.
The tool doesn't know what sounds natural for this voice.
Use the setting that removes the most noise, even if the voice sounds thin.
An over-cleaned voice sounds fake and distracts viewers.
B10.why: Listen before and after. Your ears decide.

B10.q: You recorded an interview next to a busy road. What’s the best fix?
options: Re-record somewhere quieter if you can, then clean up what’s left.
Keep the road take and let AI clean-up remove all the traffic.
AI can't fully remove it without harming the voice.
Add music over the interview so the traffic is harder to notice.
Music covers noise but also competes with the voice.
Turn the voice up so the traffic seems quieter by comparison.
Turning up the voice raises the traffic with it.
B10.why: Good sound starts at the recording. AI is the backup.

B11.q: You filmed a bride at a family wedding. Her white saree looks like a flat white patch, and you cannot see its pattern. What do you do?
options: Lower the highlights until the saree pattern shows again.
Raise the exposure so the saree looks brighter.
It is already too bright; more makes the white patch bigger.
Raise the saturation so the saree looks richer.
Saturation changes colour, not the lost pattern in the white.
Lift the shadows so the whole frame looks even.
Shadows aren't the problem; the bright white is.
B11.why: Highlights are the brightest parts of the picture. Bringing them down can bring back detail in white areas that look blank.

B11.q: In the Adobe video, how is the Auto correction button best used?
options: As a quick first step that you then adjust by hand.
As a complete fix you can trust without checking.
Auto only makes a guess; check it.
As a way to match this clip to the other clips automatically.
Auto looks at one clip only.
As a way to add a creative style to the clip.
Auto aims for a neutral look, not a style.
B11.why: The video shows Auto first, then the manual controls. Auto gives you a starting point, and your eyes decide the final result.

B11.q: You film an evening puja at home under yellow bulbs. On your phone, the white wall behind the family looks orange. What do you do?
options: Move the temperature cooler until the wall looks neutral.
Move the temperature warmer until the wall looks neutral.
Warmer adds even more orange.
Lower the saturation until the orange fades.
That drains all colour and leaves a dull cast, not a neutral wall.
Lower the brightness until the orange looks softer.
Darker doesn't change the colour cast.
B11.why: Yellow bulbs give warm light. Cooling the temperature cancels the orange so the wall looks the way it does to your eyes.

B11.q: Why does the StudioBinder video stress keeping white balance the same between shots?
options: So the colour does not jump when you cut between shots.
So every shot gets a warm, cinematic feel.
Consistency is about matching, not about a style.
So you never need to adjust colour in the edit.
You may still need small adjustments.
So the files stay smaller and easier to edit.
White balance has nothing to do with file size.
B11.why: If white balance changes between shots, the same scene looks bluer in one and more orange in the next, which feels wrong to viewers.

B11.q: Based on the StudioBinder video, which light gives a warmer, more orange colour?
options: A regular household tungsten bulb.
Bright sunlight at midday.
Midday sun is close to neutral, not orange.
Light from a cloudy, overcast sky.
Overcast light is cooler and bluish.
Light from a white LED panel.
White LED panels are neutral or cool, not orange.
B11.why: Tungsten bulbs have a low colour temperature, around 3200 Kelvin, so they look warm and orange next to daylight.

B11.q: You filmed a vegetable stall at a street market. The brightness is fine and whites look white, but the red tomatoes look faded. What do you change?
options: Raise the saturation a little.
Raise the brightness a little.
The brightness is fine; faded colour is a saturation problem.
Move the temperature warmer.
That adds orange to everything, not richer red.
Raise the contrast a lot.
Contrast changes light and dark, but doesn't make the red richer.
B11.why: Saturation controls how strong colours are. A small boost brings back the reds without changing brightness or the white balance.

B11.q: A phone clip of your shop is too dark and also a little orange. Which do you fix first?
options: Get the light level right, then sort out the colour.
Sort out the colour, then get the light level right.
Colour is judged on a correct light level, so fix light first.
Fix both at once with a strong preset filter.
A strong preset hides the problem instead of fixing it.
Fix only the colour; the dark look suits a shop.
Too dark hides detail and weakens the colour.
B11.why: Colours are hard to judge in a picture that is too dark. Fixing brightness first gives you a true base for colour work.

B11.q: Like in the Adobe video, you press Auto and the clip looks close, but the colours now feel too loud. Which manual slider do you lower?
options: Saturation, to calm the colours down.
Contrast, to soften the darks and brights.
Contrast changes light and dark, not how loud the colours are.
Temperature, to make the clip look cooler.
Temperature shifts warm to cool; it doesn't calm colours.
Exposure, to make everything darker.
Exposure changes brightness, not colour strength.
B11.why: The video shows manual controls for fine-tuning after Auto. Saturation is the one that sets how strong the colours look.

B11.q: You film a tailor's interview on two phones. In the edit, one phone's shots make his face look bluer than the other's. What do you do?
options: Warm the bluer clips until his skin matches the other phone.
Leave it, because viewers will not notice the change.
Viewers feel a face colour changing at every cut.
Put a strong filter on both to hide the difference.
A filter doesn't fix the mismatch; it can make it worse.
Raise the saturation on the bluer clips to hide the cast.
More saturation boosts the blue instead of removing it.
B11.why: Shots from the same scene should look like one moment. Adjusting the odd clip toward the other keeps the cuts smooth.

B11.q: In the Adobe video, what does the Color Match tool do?
options: Copies the colour of a reference shot onto another clip.
Sets the camera's white balance while you are filming.
Color Match works in the edit, not in the camera.
Picks the best-looking clip from your whole timeline.
It doesn't judge clips; it copies a colour look.
Makes the brightness of all clips equal automatically.
It matches colour to a chosen reference, not brightness across clips.
B11.why: You choose a reference shot you like, and Color Match adjusts another clip so the two look consistent.
B11.video: Create a professional look using Color Match and Curves

B11.q: A client wants a golden, warm look for their wedding film. Some of your clips are brighter than others. What do you do first?
options: Even out the brightness across clips, then add the golden look.
Add the golden look, then fix clips that still stand out.
Fix the base first, or the look will land differently on each clip.
Add the golden look only to the darker clips.
Only some clips would be golden, so the film wouldn't match.
Add a stronger golden look to the brighter clips to balance them.
A colour look doesn't fix a brightness mismatch.
B11.why: Evening out the clips gives you a clean base. A style added on top then looks the same across the whole film.

B11.q: You are editing a promo for a small restaurant. Which change is correcting a problem rather than adding a creative look?
options: Making the plates white again in one shot that looks blue.
Turning the whole video into black and white.
That is a creative look, not a fix.
Giving all the food shots a soft, dreamy glow.
That is a creative choice, not correcting a problem.
Making the sunset behind the restaurant more orange.
That is a creative look, not a correction.
B11.why: A blue tint on white plates is an error that makes one shot stand out. Removing it is a correction, while black and white or a glow are style choices.

B12.q: You are making a 1-minute phone video for your cousin's new sweet shop. Which opening title should you use?
options: "Mehta Sweets" in big, plain letters, on screen for about 3 seconds
"Mehta Sweets" in thin, fancy letters, on screen for about 3 seconds
Thin fancy letters are hard to read on a small phone screen.
The full shop address and phone number in curly script for 1 second
Too many words in a fancy font, and 1 second is not enough to read.
"Mehta Sweets" with letters flying in one by one for 8 seconds
The animation slows the video down and pulls attention from the name.
B12.why: A few words in a plain font are easy to read, and about 3 seconds gives people time to read them without getting bored.

B12.q: The video shows how to make a lower third. What is a lower third usually used for?
options: Showing a speaker's name and role near the bottom while they talk
Placing a big title across the middle of the screen at the start
That is an opening title, not a lower third.
Listing everyone who worked on the video at the very end
Those are end credits.
Showing a quote from the speaker across the whole screen
A lower third is a small name tag at the bottom, not a full-screen quote.
B12.why: A lower third is a small text label in the bottom part of the frame. It tells viewers who is speaking without covering their face.

B12.q: You are adding a title to a wedding video. You are not sure if the groom's name is spelled "Aarav" or "Arav". What do you do?
options: Check the spelling the family sent you, or message them to confirm
Use the spelling you see most often for that name online
What is common isn't what this family uses.
Type it the way it sounds when the guests say it aloud
Spoken sounds don't show the spelling.
Pick the spelling that looks more formal for a wedding
Names have a correct spelling; don't guess.
B12.why: Only the family knows the right spelling of their own names. A quick message saves an embarrassing mistake in a video they will keep for years.

B12.q: You have finished all the titles for a small bakery's video. What is the best way to check them?
options: Read each one slowly, word by word, and ask a friend to read them too
Trust the spell check in your editing app to catch any errors
Spell check doesn't know names or catch a word that is spelled right but wrong.
Skim them quickly, since you typed them yourself just now
You read what you meant to type, so you miss your own errors.
Read each one once on your phone screen, then export
One quick read misses typos; read slowly and ask another person.
B12.why: Slow reading catches small errors, and a fresh pair of eyes spots what you have stopped seeing.

B12.q: Your phone app made automatic captions for an interview with a shopkeeper. He says "fifteen years" but the caption shows "fifty years". What do you do?
options: Play the whole clip and correct every line that differs from the audio
Fix that one line and trust the app for the rest of the clip
Other lines may be wrong too.
Re-run the automatic captions in a different app and compare
Another app has its own mistakes; only the audio is the truth.
Check only the numbers and names, and trust the rest
Any word can be wrong, not just numbers and names.
B12.why: Automatic captions often mishear words, especially numbers, names and mixed languages. You need to check every line while listening.

B12.q: In the video, what happens before the captions are created?
options: The speech is turned into written text through transcription
The caption font, colour and size are chosen first
Style comes after the words exist.
The editor types every caption by hand from memory
Captions come from transcription, not memory.
The captions are timed to the picture before any text exists
The text has to exist before it can be timed.
B12.why: Transcription means changing spoken words into written text. The captions are built from that text, so it comes first.
B12.video: Improve video accessibility using captioning tools

B12.q: A boutique owner asks you for an Instagram Reel from your 3-minute edit. How should you export it?
options: Make it tall (9:16) and trim it to under 90 seconds
Make it tall (9:16) and export the full 3 minutes
Reels are short; a 3-minute cut is too long.
Keep it wide (16:9) and trim it to under 90 seconds
A wide video appears small with black bars on a Reel.
Make it square (1:1) and trim it to under 90 seconds
Reels are tall; a square video leaves empty space.
B12.why: Reels are watched on phones held upright, and people scroll fast. A tall, short video fits the screen and holds attention.

B12.q: The video shows Quick Export. What should you set before you press export?
options: The file name, the folder it saves to, and a preset for the platform
Choose the platform preset, but keep the default file name and folder
Default names and folders make files hard to find and can overwrite earlier exports.
Only the highest quality preset, whatever the platform is
The highest quality may be too large or not suit the platform.
Only the folder it saves to, and leave the other settings
The platform preset and file name matter too.
B12.why: A preset is a ready-made group of export settings. A clear name, a known folder and the right preset mean you can find the file and it suits where it will play.
B12.video: Share your videos fast using Quick Export

B12.q: You exported a video of a family function. The preview in the editor looked fine. You are about to send it to your aunt on WhatsApp. What should you do first?
options: Play the saved file from start to end, with sound on, before sending
Send it now, since the editor preview already looked fine
The saved file can differ from the preview.
Watch the first 10 seconds of the saved file, then send it
Problems often appear later in the file.
Play it with the sound off to check the picture
Sound problems wouldn't show.
B12.why: The file you send is what your aunt will see. Checking all of it, with sound, is the only way to be sure it is right.

B12.q: While watching your exported file, you notice the captions disappear in the last minute. What do you do?
options: Fix it in the editor, export again, and watch the new file too
Send it anyway and tell them the end has no captions
You can fix it before sending.
Fix it in the editor, export again, and send without watching
The new file might have another problem; watch it.
Export again with a different preset and send whichever looks better
A different preset doesn't fix the missing captions.
B12.why: Each export makes a new file. Only by watching the new one can you be sure the fix worked and nothing else broke.

B12.q: In the subtitles video, what do you do after the captions are generated?
options: Correct the words and timing, then check they’re easy to read in the export.
Export straight away.
Auto captions are often wrong, so correct them first.
Delete them and type every caption by hand.
That wastes time when most lines are right; correct the words and timing.
Correct the words only, since timing is set by the tool.
Timing can be off too.
B12.why: Generate, correct, then check in the final video.

B12.q: Your video mixes Hindi and English. The auto captions spell the Hindi words oddly. What do you do?
options: Fix them so they read naturally for your viewers.
Leave them. People will understand.
Odd spellings distract and look careless.
Remove the Hindi words from the video.
That changes what was said.
Translate every Hindi word into English in the captions.
That changes what the speakers actually said.
B12.why: Captions should match how people really speak.

B13.q: You copied a creator's wedding film shot by shot. Your version still feels flat next to theirs. What should you check next?
options: The sounds they used, like vows, laughter and music, and where each one comes in
Whether they used a more expensive camera and lens than yours
Better gear rarely explains why a film feels alive; the choices made do.
Whether they added stronger colour filters than you did in the edit
Colour can help the look, but it seldom fixes a film that feels flat.
Whether their shots were steadier because they used a gimbal
Steadiness helps, but it doesn't explain flatness when the shots are the same.
B13.why: Sound often carries the feeling of a video, so studying what you hear and when it appears shows you a big part of the craft.

B13.q: In the bride and groom prep video, what does the filmmaker pay close attention to while the couple gets ready?
options: The people, the small details around them and the light already in the room
Setting up big extra lights so every corner of the room is bright
The filmmaker works with the light already in the room.
Getting the couple to repeat actions until each shot looks perfect
Repeating actions makes the moments feel staged, not real.
Asking the couple to look at the camera in each shot
Looking at the camera breaks the natural feeling of getting ready.
B13.why: Good prep footage mixes people and details, and it works with the natural light so the room still feels real.
B13.video: How to Film Bride and Groom Prep — Wedding BTS Part 2

B13.q: A sweet shop owner asks you for a one-minute video. He wants to show his history, every sweet, his staff, his prices and his new branch. What do you suggest?
options: Pick one thing viewers should remember, like "fresh sweets made by hand daily", and build around it
Fit everything in by using many quick shots so nothing is left out
Cramming everything in leaves viewers remembering nothing.
Make the video about the new branch, because it is the newest news
Newest is not the same as what viewers should remember.
Skip planning a point and just film the prettiest sweets in nice light
Pretty shots without a point don't stay in the mind.
B13.why: A short video works best when a viewer can sum it up in one sentence, and every shot supports that sentence.

B13.q: You filmed your cousin's mehendi. Before editing, a friend asks what the video is about. Which answer shows you are ready to edit?
options: "It shows how the whole family came together and laughed with the bride"
"It has the mehendi, the dancing, the food, the gifts and the guests"
That lists what you filmed, not what the video is about.
"It is a nice, happy video of the mehendi"
That describes the mood, not the point you are building to.
"I'll know what it is about once I finish the edit"
Without a point before editing, you don't know what to keep.
B13.why: One clear feeling in a sentence tells you which clips belong and which can go.

B13.q: You are filming a friend's small shop opening on your phone. You have only twenty minutes. What do you film first?
options: A wide view of the shop, the ribbon cutting up close and the owner's speech heard clearly
Slow-motion shots of guests walking in, the flowers and the sweets table
Pretty extras come after the shots the story needs.
Close-ups of the ribbon, the sign and the sweets, with the speech recorded from the back
A speech recorded from the back is unclear.
Rooftop angles, shots through the window and a timelapse of the street
These are extras; first cover the opening, the ribbon and the speech.
B13.why: The shots you cannot do without come first, and extras only if time is left.

B13.q: In the video on filming a ceremony alone, when should cameras and audio be set in place?
options: Before the ceremony begins, so the key moments are covered without rushing
Once the couple arrives, so you can see where they will stand
The key moments will already be starting.
After the first few minutes, once you know how the ceremony flows
You would miss the early moments, and moving gear distracts.
During quiet parts of the ceremony, moving gear when no one is looking
Moving gear in the ceremony is noisy and distracting.
B13.why: Working solo, you cannot be everywhere, so placing cameras and recorders early makes sure the must-have moments are captured.
B13.video: How to Film a Wedding Ceremony Solo

B14.q: A bakery in your area asks for a 60-second video for Instagram. You have the brief. What should you do before you pick up the phone to shoot?
options: Decide the one thing viewers must remember, then sketch a start, middle and end.
Go to the bakery and film everything, then find the story while editing.
Without a point, you will have hours of footage and no story.
Choose the music and the colour style first, then think about the shots.
Style comes after you know what the video is about.
Write out the voice-over for the whole video before choosing the message.
A script without a clear message has nothing to say.
B14.why: A clear main message and a simple shape tell you which shots you need. Everything else gets easier after that.

B14.q: You make a 1-minute video about a local tailor. Using three-act structure, which moment belongs in the middle part?
options: The tailor working through a tricky order, showing skill and effort.
The shop sign and the tailor saying hello to the camera.
That is the opening, which belongs in act one.
A happy customer trying on the finished outfit in the mirror.
That is the ending, which belongs in act three.
The tailor explaining who his regular customers are.
That sets the scene, which belongs in act one.
B14.why: The middle part develops the story. It shows the work, the problem or the change that leads to the ending.

B14.q: You are filming a small shop. The owner says they must close in 20 minutes, and you still have six shots on your list. What do you do?
options: Film the shots you marked as essential first, then add extras if time is left.
Film the shots in the order they appear on your list until time runs out.
Essential shots may be at the end of your list and get missed.
Film quick, shaky versions of all six so nothing is skipped.
Shaky shots are unusable, so nothing is really covered.
Film the shots that look best first, then the plain ones.
The best-looking shots aren't always the essential ones.
B14.why: Knowing which shots carry the video lets you protect them when time is short. Extras are a bonus.

B14.q: You are writing a shot list for your new project. What should each line on the list tell you?
options: What the shot shows, how wide or close it is, and the camera angle.
Only the name of the place where you will be filming that day.
That is a location note, not a shot.
The music track and the transition you will use in the edit.
Those are edit decisions, not shots.
The final length of the shot and where it appears in the edit.
That comes in the edit; a shot list describes what to film.
B14.why: A good shot list describes each shot clearly, so on the day you know exactly what to capture and can tick it off.

B14.q: You record a vendor speaking at a busy vegetable market on your phone. How do you get clear sound?
options: Move the phone close to the speaker, away from the noise, and listen back.
Stand back for a wide shot and raise the voice volume later in the edit.
Raising it later raises the noise too.
Ask the vendor to speak louder and trust the phone's mic from where you are.
A phone mic far away still picks up the market more than the voice.
Use the phone's zoom to get closer to the vendor from where you stand.
Zoom doesn't bring the microphone closer to the speaker.
B14.why: Distance is the biggest cause of bad phone sound. Getting the mic close and checking a test clip saves the recording.
B14.video: An Activist's Guide to Mobile Video — Sound Recording

B14.q: You watch your edit and note three problems: the voice cuts out for 5 seconds, one title is a bit small, and one shot is half a second long. What do you fix first?
options: The voice gap, because missing speech hurts every viewer.
The small title, because viewers see titles first.
A small title is a minor fix compared with missing speech.
The short shot, because it is the quickest fix.
Quick isn't the same as important.
Whichever problem you notice first when you re-watch.
Fix the most serious problem first, not the first one you spot.
B14.why: Missing sound breaks the video for everyone who watches. Fix the problem that hurts the most, then move to smaller ones.

B14.q: Your friend watches your video about a weaver and asks, "Who is this man?" What is the best response?
options: Add a name title or a short line in the video that says who he is.
Explain it to your friend and leave the video just as it is.
Viewers can't ask you; the video must explain itself.
Ask a second friend, and only change it if they are confused too.
One confused viewer is enough to show a gap.
Put his name in the video's description only.
Many viewers never read the description.
B14.why: Someone seeing the video fresh shows you gaps you cannot notice. If they are confused, others will be too.

B14.q: In your rough cut you want to put a new clip between two clips without losing any of either. Which kind of edit do you use?
options: An insert edit, which pushes the later clips along to make room.
An overwrite edit, which places the new clip at that exact point.
Overwrite replaces footage underneath; it would delete part of a clip.
A trim edit, which shortens both clips to make a gap for it.
Trimming loses part of both clips, which you wanted to keep.
A ripple delete, which removes a clip and closes the gap.
A ripple delete removes footage; it doesn't add a clip.
B14.why: Insert adds the clip and moves everything after it, so nothing is covered up. Overwrite puts the clip on top of what is there.

B14.q: You have finished a birthday video for a family friend and exported it. What do you do before you send it on WhatsApp?
options: Play the exported file from start to end with the sound turned on.
Play it once more inside the editing app, since that looked fine.
The saved file can differ from the preview.
Send it and ask them to tell you if anything looks wrong.
Problems should be found by you, not the person you send it to.
Check the file size and length in the file details, then send it.
Size and length don't show picture or sound problems.
B14.why: The exported file is what people will actually see. Watching it fully catches missing sound, cut-off endings and spelling errors.

B14.q: When you use Quick Export, why should you set the file name and where the file is saved?
options: So you can find the right file later and not mix it up with old versions.
Because a clear file name makes the picture quality higher.
A name doesn't change the quality.
Because choosing a folder makes the export finish much faster.
The folder doesn't change export speed.
Because it tells the editing app which platform to export for.
The platform is set by the preset, not the name or folder.
B14.why: A clear name and a known folder stop you from sending the wrong or older version by mistake.
B14.video: Share your videos fast using Quick Export

B-PS.q: In the talk on speaking, what helps people want to listen?
options: Speaking with honesty, clarity and a steady pace.
Speaking as fast as possible to fit more in.
Fast speech is harder to follow.
Using as many big words as you can.
Big words hide meaning and make you sound less honest.
Speaking in a deep, dramatic voice.
Drama is not honesty or clarity.
B-PS.why: Clear and honest beats long and clever.
B-PS.video: How to Speak So That People Want to Listen

B-PS.q: You have one minute to introduce yourself to a café owner. What do you include?
options: Who you are, what you make, and one example that fits them.
Every video you've ever made.
Too much; pick one that fits them.
Your camera model and settings.
Owners care about what you can do for them, not your gear.
Your prices and when you are available.
Too early; first show who you are and what fits them.

B-PS.q: In the video on asking better questions, what comes after you ask a question?
options: Listening fully, then following up on what they said.
Moving straight to your next prepared question.
You would miss what they said and any chance to follow up.
Planning your clever reply while they talk.
If you plan while they speak, you aren't listening.
Explaining what you would do.
Explaining comes after you've listened.
B-PS.why: Good questions only work if you listen to the answers.
B-PS.video: How to Ask Better Questions — The Art of Listening & Communication

B-PS.q: A client says, “I just want something nice.” What’s a good next question?
options: “Who should watch it, and what should they do afterwards?”
"Do you want it shot in 4K, or is HD enough for you?"
That is a technical detail asked too early.
"Do you want it to be funny or serious?"
Tone comes after you know who it is for and what it should do.
"OK, I'll make something nice and send it to you to see."
Guessing leads to rework; ask what it is for first.
B-PS.why: Open questions turn vague wishes into a clear goal.

B-PS.q: In the feedback talk, what makes feedback useful?
options: Specific things you noticed, not vague labels.
Saying everything is great.
That tells them nothing they can use.
Listing every mistake at once.
Too many points overwhelm; choose the most useful.
Comparing their work with a famous film to show the standard.
Comparing to a famous film isn't specific or helpful.
B-PS.why: Specific feedback is easier to hear and act on.
B-PS.video: The Secret to Giving Great Feedback

B-PS.q: Your classmate’s video has shaky shots in the middle. What’s the most useful thing to say?
options: “The shots at 0:40–1:00 shake. Try a stand or a wall to lean on.”
"It's bad. You should probably redo the whole thing."
Harsh and vague; it doesn't say what to fix.
"It's fine, honestly," so you don't hurt their feelings.
Kind but useless; they can't improve.
"The video is shaky." and nothing more.
Too vague; it doesn't say where or how to fix it.
B-PS.why: Say what you saw, where, and one idea to fix it.

B-PS.q: In the video on first client meetings, what do you set out early?
options: How you’ll work: what’s included, timing and who decides.
Your full price list, so they know the cost up front.
Price comes after the work is clear.
Your favourite filmmakers, so they can see your taste.
They want to know how you'll work with them.
A summary of your biggest past projects.
They know your work; they need to know how you work with them.
B-PS.why: Clear terms at the start prevent trouble later.
B-PS.video: Establish the Terms of Engagement During the First Client Meeting

B-PS.q: After a meeting, the client says, “Let’s talk again soon.” What do you do the same day?
options: Send a short written summary of what you agreed and what’s next.
Wait for them to call you, so you don't seem too pushy.
A written summary the same day is professional, not pushy.
Start filming straight away so you don't lose any time.
Filming before agreeing the plan risks wasted work.
Send your portfolio again so they remember you.
A summary of what you agreed is what matters.
B-PS.why: Write it down and send it the same day.

B-PS.q: In the video on landing clients with YouTube, what kind of video brings in clients?
options: One that shows how you solve a real problem for clients like them.
One showing off your newest camera.
Clients want solutions, not gear.
A long list of your services.
A list doesn't show how you solve a problem.
A vlog about your daily life as a filmmaker.
Clients want to see their own problem solved.
B-PS.why: Show the result a client wants to buy.
B-PS.video: How to Land More Clients Using YouTube! — 3 Examples

B-PS.q: You want to film for gyms. Which first sample is most useful?
options: A short video for one gym, showing its classes and members.
Your best wedding highlight film, since it shows your skill.
A wedding film doesn't show gym clients that you understand their business.
A tutorial on colour grading to show your technical level.
Gyms want to see what you'd make for them, not a tutorial.
A montage of fitness stock clips with music.
Stock isn't your work, so it proves nothing.
B-PS.why: Make the sample your future client wants to see.
